title: Make It Move
tagline: Your first physical computer reacts to you.
objectives: I can explain the difference between an input and an output using real examples.
I can build a working program on a real micro:bit that reacts to an input.
I can test my program and use what happens (or doesn't) to find and fix problems myself.

config.headline: Something happens. Something reacts.
lines: Every lift button, every pedestrian crossing, every step-counter on a wrist runs on one single idea: an INPUT triggers an OUTPUT.
Today you build your first physical computer — a real device, in your real hands, that reacts when you tell it to.
By the end of the hour it will answer your button press, and even your shake, with light signals of its own.

config.title: The Signal Relay Ladder
config.intro: Four rungs. Each one is a target behaviour your pair must make REAL on the micro:bit in your hands. Nobody marks this — the device itself is the judge. Take turns: one of you builds the blocks, the other holds the card and presses the button to test. Swap every rung.

unplugged.title: Rung 1 — The Human Circuit
lines: Stand up with your partner. One of you is the SENSOR, the other is the ACTUATOR. No screens for this rung — you two ARE the machine.
SENSOR: mime pressing an invisible button. ACTUATOR: the instant you see it, throw your arms up — that's your LED heart lighting.
New input: SENSOR mimes shaking a device. ACTUATOR: wave both hands — that's your scrolling message.
Swap roles and run both signals again.
Now say it out loud together: the press is the INPUT. The reaction is the OUTPUT. The rule connecting them — when THIS happens, do THAT — is an EVENT.
unplugged.confirm: We both played Sensor and Actuator — and said the magic sentence
soloLines: No screens for this rung — and no partner needed on a catch-up: YOU are the whole machine.
With one hand, mime pressing an invisible button. The instant you do, throw your other arm up — that's your LED heart lighting.
New input: mime shaking a device with one hand — wave the other — that's your scrolling message.
Now say it out loud (quietly counts): the press is the INPUT. The reaction is the OUTPUT. The rule connecting them — when THIS happens, do THAT — is an EVENT.
unplugged.soloConfirm: I ran both signals — and said the magic sentence

rungs.title: Rung 2 — First Signal
rungs.target: On button A pressed → show a HEART icon.
rungs.test: Flash it to the micro:bit, then press the REAL button A (or the on-screen simulator if your device is sulking). Did the heart appear?
rungs.hint: Is your 'show icon' block sitting INSIDE the 'on button A pressed' block? A block floating on its own never runs.

rungs.title: Rung 3 — Two Signals
rungs.target: Button A shows a HEART. Button B shows a HAPPY face. Two inputs, two different outputs.
rungs.test: Press A, then B, on the device. Do you get two DIFFERENT icons?
rungs.hint: You need TWO separate 'on button pressed' blocks — one set to A, one set to B. Check the little dropdown on each one.

rungs.title: Rung 4 — The Vanishing Ghost
rungs.target: On shake → show the ghost icon, hold it on screen for one second, then clear the screen.
rungs.test: Give it a real shake. Does the ghost appear, hold, then vanish cleanly — every single time? Now the proof it matters: DELETE the pause block and shake again. The ghost never gets a chance to appear at all. Put the pause back.
rungs.hint: The ORDER inside 'on shake' matters: show icon, THEN pause (ms) 1000, THEN clear screen. The pause is the only thing giving the ghost time on screen — without it, 'clear screen' wipes it before your eyes can catch it and you see nothing at all. (Rung 2's heart stayed put because nothing came along to clear it.)

stretch.title: Stretch — Compound Signal
stretch.target: Press A + B TOGETHER → heart, a half-second pause, then a happy face. One input, a whole light sequence.
stretch.test: Press A + B together on the real device — heart, half-second pause, then happy face. Every single time?

config.introSolo: Four rungs. Each is a target behaviour YOU make real on a micro:bit (or the on-screen simulator) — catch-up solo mission, so you do every job yourself: build the blocks AND run the real test. Nobody marks this: the device itself is the judge.

config.title: Bank your build
config.intro: A build that lives on one computer is a build you can lose. Agents bank their work in the Vault — then it follows your login to ANY machine, even at home.

steps.title: Download your build
steps.text: In MakeCode press the purple Download button. A file ending in .hex lands in the computer's Downloads folder — that file IS your program.

steps.title: Open your Vault
steps.text: New tab → drive.google.com → open School → DT Work. Don't see those folders? Tap + New → Folder, make 'School', open it, make 'DT Work' inside — thirty seconds, then carry on.

steps.title: Drag it in
steps.text: Drag the .hex file from Downloads into DT Work. Done — HQ can now verify it's really there.

config.passText: Your build now follows your login anywhere — that's the whole point of the Vault. Next lesson you can pick up exactly where you left off, on any machine.
config.failText: Not there yet. Check each step above — especially that the file went INTO the DT Work folder, not just onto the desktop — then run the inspection again.

config.intro: One scenario before you clock off, Agent — think like a debugger.

items.stem: You build 'on button A pressed → show heart'. You press button A on the micro:bit but nothing appears. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: You forgot to flash the code onto the device
Button A only works if you press button B at the same time

items.stem: Your finished program: press button A → a heart appears on the LED grid. Which part is the INPUT?

statements: I can tell the difference between an input and an output.
I can build code that reacts when something happens.
I can test my code and notice when it's not working.
